versions.text:
Barley and the Falling Light

Once, in a starlit meadow, a young bear cub named Barley sat by a pond. The pond was so still it held the whole sky inside it.

Barley had a plan. Tonight he would catch a shooting star for his mother.

"Mama likes bright things," he said to himself. "A star would make her smile."

Beside him sat Grandmother Shell, an old turtle with a mossy back and kind, slow eyes.

"Grandmother Shell, will you help me catch a star?" asked Barley.

Grandmother Shell blinked. "Stars are very far away, little one. But let us look for one together."

So they waited. The grass was soft and cool. Crickets sang in the reeds. A frog said, "Plip." A breeze smelled of clover and rain.

Suddenly, a streak of light zipped across the sky!

"There!" cried Barley, jumping up. He ran along the edge of the pond. He leaned so far that his nose almost touched the water. He reached and reached.

Splash! Barley tumbled in. He came up sputtering, with a leaf on his head.

Grandmother Shell did not laugh. She only waited, patient as the hills.

"The star is not in the water, Barley," she said gently. "Look up, and you will see it in the pond too."

Barley sat down on the bank, dripping. He looked up. High above, a silver light still glimmered.

Then he looked down. There it was again, shining in the still water, right beside a reflected moon.

"Oh," said Barley softly. "It is in both places at once."

"Yes," said Grandmother Shell. "Some lovely things cannot be held. They can only be seen. And seeing them is a kind of gift."

Barley thought about this for a long time. His paws were cold, but his heart felt warm.

"Then I will give Mama the gift of seeing," he decided. "I will tell her all about it. And I will show her the star in the pond."

"That is a wise plan," said Grandmother Shell, and her eyes crinkled.

The breeze grew slow and quiet. The crickets sang more softly. The frog stopped its plipping and sat very still.

Barley yawned a big, round yawn. "Grandmother Shell, may I stay and watch a little longer?"

"You may," she said. "Just watch, and breathe, and let the sky keep you company."

So Barley lay down on the soft grass. He tucked his dripping paws under his chin. Grandmother Shell settled beside him, humming an old, sleepy tune.

Up above, the stars twinkled. Down below, they twinkled again in the pond.

Barley's eyes grew heavy. His breathing slowed, soft and steady.

"Goodnight, sky," he murmured. "Goodnight, pond. Goodnight, Grandmother Shell."

And Grandmother Shell whispered back, "Goodnight, little bear."

The meadow hushed. The stars kept their watch. And Barley slept, warm and safe, with the sky shining in his dreams.
